name: Aadanainathar Temple, Tiruvadanai
deity: Shiva as Aadanainathar (Adhi Ratneswarar), with the goddess Snehavalli
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of the Pandya country, sung in the Tevaram (7th century); the present temple reflects extensive later renovation
dynasty: Pandya country; later renovation credited to the Sethupathis (Bhaskara Sethupathi)
summary: Aadanainathar, also known as Adhi Ratneswarar, is the Lord of Tiruvadanai in the Pandya country, praised in Sambandar's hymn and remembered for the restoration of Varuna, in a vast temple with a nine-tiered gopuram and a hall of nearly three hundred pillars.

sections.history: Tiruvadanai, in Ramanathapuram district, is the Tiruvadanai of the Tevaram, one of the fourteen Paadal Petra Sthalams of the Pandya country, sung in the hymn of Sambandar. Sources differ on its place in the sequence of Pandya shrines, but agree on its standing among the sung temples. The Lord is known as Aadanainathar and, in the Sanskrit form, Adhi Ratneswarar, the first jewel; the goddess is Snehavalli, called Anbayi Ammai in Tamil. The temple stands on a very large site of about ten acres, and major renovations are credited to Bhaskara Sethupathi of the Sethupathi line. We did not find detailed records of the beginnings of the present structures in the sources we could consult, so the temple is best understood as a Tevaram-era shrine kept in continuous worship and enlarged in later centuries.
sections.architecture: The temple stands on about ten acres and is entered beneath a nine-tiered rajagopuram of roughly 130 feet, rich in stucco figures. Within is a pillared hall, the Chokkatanchari mandapam, with 291 carved pillars. The sanctum holds the linga of Aadanainathar, with the goddess Snehavalli worshipped as his consort. The sacred tank is the Surya Pushkarini, the temple's vilwa theertham, and the vilwa (bael) tree is the sacred tree. Several other sacred springs belong to the temple, named for Varuna, Vaaruni, Markandeya, Agastya and Kamadhenu.
sections.legends: The town's name is tied to the story of Varuna, the god of rain. Cursed by a sage to bear the body of an elephant and the head of a goat, he came to this temple, worshipped Shiva and regained his proper form, and the name Tiruvadanai is said to preserve the memory of that episode, the goat (aadu) and elephant (aanai) joined in one. A second telling speaks of Vaaruni, the son of Varuna, who disturbed the penance of the sage Durvasa, sought forgiveness, and was advised to pray at this temple. From these accounts the temple keeps the memory of a Lord who restores what has been broken, and the springs named for Varuna and Vaaruni recall them.
sections.festivals: The annual Brahmotsavam is held in the Tamil month of Vaikasi (May to June). The goddess is honoured with a festival in the month of Aadi, and Arudra Darisanam and Karthikai Deepam are observed, along with the Kailasa Kaatchi festival that recalls the vision of Kailasa granted to Sundarar. Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are observed as at every Shiva temple. Sources differ on the length of these festivals, so confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Tiruvadanai is a temple of generous scale, and it rewards a visit without hurry. Enter beneath the tall nine-tiered gopuram, walk the long pillared hall, and come to the sanctum of Aadanainathar before turning to the goddess Snehavalli. Many devotees pause for a while beside the Surya Pushkarini. The temple is a fitting place for those who seek the restoring of what was lost, in the spirit of Varuna's story. The town is small and quiet, and being some distance from larger towns, it is worth allowing generous time for the road.

visit.timings: Typically open from about 6:00 am to noon and again from about 4:30 pm to 8:30 pm; the listing is a few years old, so confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Tiruvadanai is a taluk town in Ramanathapuram district, about 45 km from Karaikudi by way of Devakottai, with buses from Karaikudi and Sivagangai. Tiruppunavasal, another Paadal Petra Sthalam, lies about 21 km away. The nearest railway station and airport are not confirmed in our sources, so check locally.
